speaker: Witches
quote: Fair is foul and foul is fair
sheet_note: the witches casting a spell – represents their plan to cause the collapse of society
student_note: The witches open the play with this chant. Good and evil are mixed up, which introduces the theme of disorder.
techniques: Paradox; Alliteration; Fricative; Repetition; Rhyming couplet
technique_notes: Paradox – "fair" & "foul" are opposites. This shows that in the world of the play, good and evil are blurred and turned upside down. The contrast suggests appearances are untrustworthy. | Alliteration of "f" – Creates a hissing sound, like a snake, connoting evil (devil / Adam & Eve). | Fricative – the repeated "f" sounds in "fair" and "foul" are made by air being forced through a narrow gap, creating an airy, breathless sound that suggests a spell. | Repetition – "fair" and "foul" each appear twice, with the words swapped round in the second half. The echo makes the line sound like a chant or spell and stresses how good and evil are tangled together. | Rhyming couplet – The witches speak in rhyme, creating the sound of a spell.
context: The witches open the play with this chant, introducing the theme of disorder.
lesson_techniques: Adjective “foul”; Sibilance of “f” sound; Adjective “Fair”; Chiasmus; Trochaic tetrameter and rhyme

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Stars hide your fires, let not light see my black and deep desires

He wants darkness to conceal his thoughts. | Symbolism of "stars" and "light" – Represent God, truth, and morality. | Metaphor "black desires" – Darkness connotes evil and sin. | Adjective "deep" – Suggests his ambition is buried within him and cannot easily be removed.
context: Macbeth says this in an aside after Duncan names Malcolm as his heir. Macbeth realises he must hide his ambition to become king.
lesson_techniques: Imperative “hide your fires”; Metaphor “black” desires; Symbol “stars”; Adjective “deep”

speaker: Macbeth

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Vaulting ambition which overleaps itself and falls

technique_notes: Personification – “Vaulting ambition”: Ambition is personified as something external to Macbeth, driving him upwards. | Metaphor – Suggests ambition pushes him beyond limits. | Verb "falls" – Foreshadows his eventual downfall. | Tragic Structure – Reveals Macbeth's hamartia (fatal flaw). | Hamartia – “overleaps itself and falls”: Macbeth’s fatal flaw is his ambition, which pushes him too far and causes his own downfall.
context: Macbeth debates whether to kill Duncan. He admits ambition is his only motivation.
lesson_techniques: Verb “overleaps”; Personification “Vaulting ambition”; Verb “falls”; Pivotal moment

speaker: Lady Macbeth

Attacking a child emphasises Hyde’s evil, exaggerating his callous and indiscriminate cruelty.

Hyde belongs to evil. | Imagery – “Satan’s signature”: Hellish, religious imagery of the Devil marking a face makes Hyde seem damned and evil. A signature shows who made something, implying Hyde is Satan’s creation and embodies evil.

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: His face became suddenly black and the features seemed to melt
sheet_note: Dr Lanyon describes the supernatural transformation he witnessed
student_note: Dr Lanyon describes the transformation he saw. It seems almost supernatural.
lesson_techniques: Colour imagery

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: “O God!” I screamed. “O God!”
sheet_note: Dr Lanyon describing his shock at witnessing the transformation
student_note: Dr Lanyon cries out in horror as he witnesses the transformation.
lesson_techniques: Repetition “O God!”; Verb “screamed”; Exclamative statement; Address to God

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: The deadliest terror sits by my side at all hours
sheet_note: Dr Lanyon describes the way he has been traumatised by his experience
student_note: Dr Lanyon is traumatised by what he saw. He says terror follows him everywhere.
lesson_techniques: Hyperbole “at all hours”; Personification; Emotive language “terror”; Superlative “deadliest”; Dramatic irony

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: Man is not truly one, but truly two
sheet_note: Dr Jekyll describing the duality of human nature
student_note: Jekyll explains his theory about human nature. This is the central idea of the novel, that everyone has a good side and a bad side. He sounds confident and scientific.
techniques: Declarative statement; Repetition; Juxtaposition / contrast; Noun
technique_notes: Declarative statement: Sounds confident and scientific. | Repetition – “truly”: Emphasises certainty and conviction. | Juxtaposition / contrast – “not… one… but… two”: Mirrors Jekyll’s internal conflict. | Noun – “Man”: Universalises Jekyll’s idea to all of humanity.
context: Jekyll explains his theory about human nature. He reveals the central theme of the novel: duality of good and evil within humans.

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: It was the curse of mankind that these polar twins should be continuously struggling
sheet_note: Dr Jekyll describing the conflict between good and evil within all humans
student_note: Dr Jekyll describes the conflict between good and evil inside every person. He says it is a curse that the two are bound together.
lesson_techniques: Present tense verb “struggling”; Personification “polar twins”; Metaphor “curse”; Adverb “continuously”

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: The body of Edward Hyde had grown in stature
sheet_note: Dr Jekyll describing how Mr Hyde is growing, representing how his evil nature is growing
student_note: Dr Jekyll describes Hyde growing bigger. This shows his evil side getting stronger.
lesson_techniques: Verb “grown”; Symbol: Hyde’s short height; Third person “Edward Hyde” (not “me”)

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: My new power tempted me until I fell in slavery
sheet_note: Dr Jekyll describing how his temptation led him towards his downfall. The sheet said “fell into slavery”; changed to the novel’s “fell in slavery” (teacher decision, 15 Oct)
student_note: Dr Jekyll describes how temptation led to his downfall. His new power made him a slave to Hyde.
lesson_techniques: Verb “fell”; Hyperbole “my new power”; Verb “tempted”; Metaphor “slavery”

speaker: Narrator
quote: Windows barred with iron
sheet_note: this describes Dr Jekyll’s cabinet. It seems Hellish and cage-like (on the sheet this shares an entry with “Red baize door”). Checked against the novel: this phrase is in Chapter 5, not Chapter 8
student_note: This describes Dr Jekyll's cabinet. It seems hellish and cage-like.
lesson_techniques: Symbolism of caging and repression (semantic field of cages)

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring
sheet_note: Added from the Year 11 Summer Revision document (not on the homework sheets). Wording changed to the novel’s and Lesson 23’s “had been long caged” (the document said “had long been caged”; teacher decision, 15 Oct).
student_note: Jekyll describes how Hyde burst out after years of being held back. 'Devil' shows Hyde stands for pure evil, and that evil you repress can come back stronger.
techniques: Metaphor; Possessive pronoun; Metaphor; Verb; Foreshadowing
technique_notes: Metaphor – “devil”: Hyde symbolises pure evil. | Possessive pronoun – “my”: Jekyll takes ownership of that evil. | Metaphor – “caged”: Suggests repression and imprisonment. | Verb – “roaring”: Animal imagery. Violence and power. | Foreshadowing: Suggests repression of desires eventually leads to explosion & loss of control.
context: Jekyll describes how Hyde emerged after years of repression. Repressed evil has grown stronger and more uncontrollable.
lesson_techniques: Possessive pronoun “my”; Metaphor “roaring” (a predator; Darwinian view); Semantic field of cages (links to the barred windows of Jekyll’s cabinet); Bestial imagery around Hyde

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Lighting should be pink and intimate
sheet_note: describes the cosy lighting, representing the comfortable life they lead and the façade of respectability they create
student_note: The warm pink lighting shows the comfortable life the Birlings lead and the respectable image they put on.
technique_notes: The warm “pink” lighting establishes the Birling family’s sheltered, rose-tinted complacency and the fragile domestic façade of bourgeois respectability. The sharp shift to “brighter and harder” mimics the cold glare of an interrogation lamp, visually peeling back their domestic privacy to expose their moral failings.
context: Opening stage directions signalling the shift when Inspector Goole rings the bell.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Brighter and harder
sheet_note: describes how the lighting changes when the Inspector arrives, representing the harsh and uncomfortable truth he reveals about the Birlings
student_note: When the Inspector arrives the lighting becomes harsh. This shows the uncomfortable truth he is about to reveal.
technique_notes: The warm “pink” lighting establishes the Birling family’s sheltered, rose-tinted complacency and the fragile domestic façade of bourgeois respectability. The sharp shift to “brighter and harder” mimics the cold glare of an interrogation lamp, visually peeling back their domestic privacy to expose their moral failings.
context: Opening stage directions signalling the shift when Inspector Goole rings the bell.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Substantial and heavily comfortable, but not cosy and homelike
sheet_note: describes the set – a very luxurious home but shows how the Birlings who live there lack the warmth and affection of a loving family
student_note: The room is very comfortable but not homely. The Birlings are wealthy but lack warmth and affection as a family.
technique_notes: Priestley uses the domestic environment to reflect the hollow foundations of the household. It is a space built entirely for status, expense, and material weight (“substantial”), yet completely lacks genuine warmth, affection, or emotional intimacy (“not cosy”).
context: Initial description of the dining-room interior.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: A prosperous manufacturer
sheet_note: describes Mr Birling. He’s a wealthy capitalist that owns factories
student_note: This describes Mr Birling. He is a wealthy capitalist who owns factories.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Provincial in his speech
sheet_note: describes Mr Birling’s accent, suggesting he comes from a poorer background, possibly working-class. Shows he is an ambitious, self-made businessman who wants to climb the social ladder. The play text we have reads “rather provincial in this speech” (that copy has typos); the sheet’s “in his speech” is kept
student_note: This describes Mr Birling's accent. It suggests he comes from a poorer background and has worked his way up, so he is not from the upper class.
technique_notes: Identifies Birling as nouveau riche – a self-made northern manufacturer who lacks the inherited aristocratic polish of his wife. His regional accent underscores an underlying class anxiety, explaining his obsessive desire for status symbols, boardrooms, and a knighthood.
context: Opening stage direction describing Mr Birling’s vocal delivery and manner.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: A rather cold woman
sheet_note: describes Mrs Birling. Suggests she is cold-hearted and lacks compassion and empathy
student_note: This describes Mrs Birling. It suggests she is cold-hearted and lacks compassion, which prepares us for how she treats Eva.
technique_notes: Foreshadows her moral callousness, rigid social snobbery, and total absence of maternal or civic empathy, establishing her immediately as an unyielding defender of class boundaries.
context: Opening stage direction introducing Sybil Birling.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Her husband’s social superior
sheet_note: describes Mrs Birling. She comes from upper-class aristocracy but has had to marry a wealthy middle-class businessman
student_note: This describes Mrs Birling. She comes from a higher class than her husband, so she looks down on others.
technique_notes: Establishes that Sybil comes from old, landed gentry, marrying down commercially while Arthur marries up socially. This imbalance keeps Arthur insecure and makes Sybil the strict domestic guardian of aristocratic decorum.
context: Opening stage direction defining Sybil Birling’s pedigree.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Very pleased with life and rather excited
sheet_note: describes Sheila Birling. It suggests that she is “pleased” with the sheltered, privileged life she leads, and is particularly excited by her engagement to Gerald
student_note: This describes Sheila. She is pleased with her sheltered, privileged life and is excited about her engagement.
technique_notes: Highlights Sheila’s initial naivety, sheltered privilege, and self-centred domestic focus. Priestley establishes this baseline of shallow contentment so her subsequent moral awakening (anagnorisis) carries maximum dramatic force.
context: Opening stage direction during the engagement dinner.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Easy, well-bred young man-about-town
sheet_note: describes Gerald Croft. Highlights how he is a respected gentleman in the community who comes from a highly regarded upper-class family
student_note: This describes Gerald Croft. He is a polished, respected gentleman from a wealthy upper-class family.
technique_notes: Captures Gerald’s effortless polish, charm, and elite confidence. The label “man-about-town” hints at moral carelessness, foreshadowing his casual exploitation of working-class women under the guise of gentlemanly gallantry.
context: Opening stage direction describing Gerald.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Not quite at ease, half shy, half assertive
sheet_note: describes Eric Birling. Highlights how uncomfortable he seems, perhaps because he has a distant relationship with his family or perhaps because he is hiding a secret
student_note: This describes Eric. He seems uncomfortable and uneasy, perhaps because he has a distant relationship with his family.
technique_notes: Signals Eric’s deep internal conflict, alienation from his overbearing father, and underlying instability. The friction between “shy” and “assertive” hints at repressed guilt and an explosive lack of emotional self-control.
context: Opening stage direction describing Eric.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: We may look forward to the time when Crofts and Birlings are no longer competing but are working together – for lower costs and higher prices
sheet_note: Mr Birling treats the engagement like a business deal between his family and the Crofts
student_note: Mr Birling treats the engagement like a business deal between his family and the Crofts.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: We hard-headed, practical businessmen
sheet_note: Mr Birling believes he is practical and sensible, but also shows he does not value sympathy or compassion for others. His only concern is making money, not helping society
student_note: Mr Birling thinks he is practical and sensible, but he shows he has no sympathy for others. All he cares about is making money.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable
sheet_note: Mr Birling believes that the Titanic will never sink, highlighting his arrogance and foolishness
student_note: Mr Birling is sure the Titanic will never sink. Priestley makes him look arrogant and foolish, because the audience knows it did.
technique_notes: Priestley deliberately demolishes Birling’s credibility with the 1945 audience from the outset. Birling’s foolish belief in commercial and technological invulnerability directly mirrors his blindness to the impending catastrophe of two world wars. | Repetition – “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable”: Birling’s repeated, emphatic boast shows his arrogant overconfidence in progress. | Dramatic irony – The 1945 audience knows the Titanic sank, so Birling’s certainty makes him look foolish and undermines his judgement.
context: Pontificating about industrial progress and the Titanic to Gerald and Eric.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Like bees in a hive – community and all that nonsense
sheet_note: Mr Birling makes sarcastic comments about socialist ideas, showing how he is capitalist
student_note: Mr Birling mocks socialist ideas about working together. This shows he is a capitalist who puts money first.
technique_notes: Birling trivialises collective solidarity as chaotic, insect-like conformity. By branding social responsibility as “nonsense”, his unbridled individualism acts as the moral cue that summons the Inspector’s doorbell. (The sheet also lists “Cranks” with this quote.)
context: Dismissing socialist principles immediately before Goole arrives.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: A man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own
sheet_note: Mr Birling lectures Gerald and Eric, revealing how he thinks people should be selfish
student_note: Mr Birling lectures Gerald and Eric. He thinks people should look after themselves and not worry about others.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Well, it’s my duty to keep labour costs down
sheet_note: Mr Birling explaining to the Inspector why he refused to give Eva Smith fairer pay
student_note: Mr Birling tells the Inspector why he refused to pay Eva Smith more. He says his duty is to keep costs down, not to care about workers.
techniques: Subversion of the abstract noun “duty” / capitalist ideology.
technique_notes: Birling redefines moral “duty” as purely economic self-interest and profit preservation. In his world, civic and human obligations are entirely subordinated to balance sheets and shareholder margins.
context: Justifying refusing Eva Smith and her fellow strikers fair wages.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: If you don’t come down sharply on some of these people, they’d soon be asking for the earth
sheet_note: Mr Birling justifies why he fired Eva Smith, showing a lack of empathy towards her
student_note: Mr Birling explains why he fired Eva Smith. He shows no empathy and thinks workers must be punished for asking for more money.
technique_notes: Birling presents a modest plea for twenty-five shillings a week as an existential rebellion. His punitive phrasing (“come down sharply”) treats working-class employees not as human collaborators, but as an unruly mass requiring constant suppression.
context: Defending his decision to discharge Eva Smith.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: It’s better to ask for the earth than to take it
sheet_note: The Inspector’s quick response to Mr Birling. He challenges Mr Birling’s views, showing how Capitalists often selfishly “take” from others with no regard for the impact it has
student_note: The Inspector answers Mr Birling sharply. He says the rich often take far more than the poor ever ask for, and with no thought for others.
technique_notes: Goole contrasts the humble petitions of impoverished workers (“ask”) with the aggressive, entitled plunder of capitalist factory owners (“take”), framing capitalist accumulation as institutionalised theft.
context: Direct counter to Birling’s complaint about striking workers.

speaker: Sheila
quote: Look – Mummy – isn’t it a beauty?
sheet_note: Sheila describing how beautiful her engagement ring is. Highlights how superficial and spoilt she is. Also, the way she says “Mummy” and “Daddy” highlights how childish and sheltered she is
student_note: Sheila admires her engagement ring. This shows how superficial and spoilt she is at the start. Calling her parents 'Mummy' and 'Daddy' makes her seem childlike.
technique_notes: Illustrates Sheila’s opening state of infantilised dependence. Her excitement is tied directly to an expensive commodity, viewing affection through the lens of bourgeois consumerism.
context: Admiring her diamond engagement ring.

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Nothing to do with you, Sheila. Run along
sheet_note: Mr Birling tries to exclude Sheila from conversation with the Inspector. Perhaps shows how he regards women as emotionally fragile. Also, highlights how he treats her like a child
student_note: Mr Birling tries to shut Sheila out of the conversation. He sees women as too delicate and treats her like a child.
technique_notes: Demonstrates the Edwardian patronisation of women, treating them as emotionally fragile ornaments to be shielded from public realities, while seeking to prevent younger family members from witnessing moral scrutiny.
context: Attempting to dismiss Sheila when the Inspector begins interrogating him.

speaker: Sheila
quote: I can’t help thinking about this girl destroying herself – and I’ve been so happy tonight
sheet_note: Sheila feeling sorry for Eva. The two characters are foils (contrasting characters), both young women who have faced very different lives because of their social class
student_note: Sheila feels sorry for Eva. They are both young women, but their lives are very different because of their class.

speaker: Sheila
quote: But these girls aren’t cheap labour – they’re people
sheet_note: Sheila challenges her father’s capitalist views. She humanises the working class and sees them as “people”. This contrasts to Mr Birling who sees them as “labour” to simply use and exploit
student_note: Sheila challenges her father's capitalist views. She sees the girls as people, but he sees them only as cheap labour.
technique_notes: Marks Sheila’s decisive moral shift. By replacing her father’s dehumanising economic label (“cheap labour”) with “people”, she strips away capitalist doublespeak to assert common human value.
context: Reacting to the news of Eva Smith’s dismissal from the factory.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: So you used the power you had… to punish the girl?
sheet_note: The Inspector interrogates Sheila. Sheila abused her power to make sure Eva was fired from Milwards. She was jealous and angry that Eva suited a dress that did not look good on her
student_note: The Inspector questions Sheila. She used her power to get Eva fired from Milwards because she was jealous that Eva looked better in a dress.

speaker: Sheila
quote: (laughs rather hysterically) Why – you fool – he knows. Of course he knows
sheet_note: Sheila telling Gerald he is foolish if he thinks he can lie to the Inspector. She knows that it is better to be honest and to accept the guilt for what they have done
student_note: Sheila tells Gerald he is foolish to think he can lie to the Inspector. She knows it is better to be honest and accept the blame.
technique_notes: Sheila sheds her submissive domestic role and echoes the Inspector’s incisive clarity. She recognises Goole not as an ordinary police officer, but as an omniscient moral force whom it is impossible to deceive.
context: Confronting Gerald at the end of Act 1 over Daisy Renton.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Inspector Goole
sheet_note: The Inspector’s name, “Goole” is a homophone for “ghoul”, meaning ghost. This could represent how he has supernatural powers or could be symbolic of God and the Holy Ghost
student_note: 'Goole' sounds like 'ghoul', which means ghost. This could suggest the Inspector has supernatural powers or that he is like a conscience.
technique_notes: “Goole” is an explicit homophone for “ghoul”, evoking a spirit or supernatural entity that feasts on the dead. This positions him beyond mortal policing: he acts as an uncanny, metaphysical harbinger, a manifestation of the collective guilt of the Birlings, or an emissary of divine judgment.
context: The name of the central inquisitor.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Cutting in, massively
sheet_note: stage direction describing how the Inspector interrupts the Birlings and Gerald while they speak. Emphasises how he is a strong, powerful force that cannot be overcome
student_note: The Inspector interrupts the Birlings and Gerald. This shows he is a strong force who takes control of the room.
technique_notes: The Inspector asserts total narrative and physical control over the stage. “Cutting in” disrupts the patriarchal family hierarchy, while “massively” conveys an immovable, monolithic moral force that Birling’s civic status cannot intimidate or derail.
context: Repeated stage direction governing Goole’s interruptions of Birling.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: He speaks carefully, weightily
sheet_note: stage directions describing how the Inspector speaks. He speaks carefully because he is in control of both his words and the situation. Also, his words carry much power and importance
student_note: This describes how the Inspector speaks. He is careful and calm because he is in control of his words and of the situation.
technique_notes: Contrasts sharply with Birling’s excitable, arrogant rambling. Goole’s deliberate, measured delivery establishes intellectual and moral command; every phrase carries philosophical weight and judicial gravity.
context: Opening stage direction introducing the Inspector’s manner of speech.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: A chain of events
sheet_note: The Inspector describes how not one factor, but numerous factors, all contributed to Eva’s death. This highlights how each of them are responsible
student_note: The Inspector says many different people helped cause Eva's death. This shows each of them is responsible.
technique_notes: Introduces Priestley’s core disciplinary concept of causality. Each individual cruelty acts as an interlocking link, demonstrating that moral accountability is cumulative and that seemingly minor acts of selfishness produce devastating collective consequences.
context: Goole explaining how individual actions contributed to Eva’s suicide.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Eva Smith
sheet_note: Eva’s name is significant. The surname “Smith” is a common, working-class surname, suggesting she represents the working class. “Eva” is a variation of “Eve”, the first woman created by God in the Bible, suggesting she represents the experiences of working-class women
student_note: 'Smith' is a very common working-class surname, so Eva stands for all working-class people. 'Eva' is a form of Eve, the first woman in the Bible.
technique_notes: “Eva” recalls Eve (the biblical mother of all living humanity), while “Smith” is the most common British working-class surname, transforming her into an Everyman figure for the labouring masses. “Daisy” evokes a common, easily crushed field flower, while “Renton” hints at the financial desperation that forced her to rent out her body to survive.
context: The two names used by the victim across the narrative.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: She’d swallowed a lot of strong disinfectant. Burnt her inside out
sheet_note: The Inspector describing how Eva Smith died. It was a very violent and gruesome suicide
student_note: The Inspector describes how Eva died. It was a violent and gruesome suicide, and he wants the family to hear every detail.
techniques: Visceral sensory imagery / graphic physical description.
technique_notes: The grotesque, physical detail of being “burnt inside out” shatters the polite, sanitised atmosphere of the dining room. Disinfectant cleanses surface dirt; Eva using it internally acts as a horrific metaphor for a desperate, corrupted society destroying itself from within.
context: The Inspector bluntly describing Eva Smith’s suicide to the family in Act 1.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: No relatives to help her, few friends, lonely, half-starved, she was feeling desperate
sheet_note: The Inspector describing Eva when she was unemployed for two months after Mr Birling fired her from the factory. “Half-starved” shows how impoverished she is, contrasting to the Birlings who are enjoying fine dining to celebrate Sheila and Gerald’s engagement
student_note: The Inspector describes Eva after Mr Birling fired her. She had no family, few friends and almost no money, and there was no help for the poor.
technique_notes: The cumulative list of privations highlights the absolute absence of a social safety net in 1912 Edwardian Britain. “Half-starved” sharply contrasts with the Birlings’ lavish port and dinner party, exposing the lethal consequences of capitalist abandonment.
context: Goole recounting Eva’s period of unemployment after Birling fired her.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: It would do us all a bit of good if we put ourselves in the place of these young women counting their pennies in their dingy little back bedrooms
sheet_note: The Inspector speaking to the Birlings. He suggests that it is important to show empathy to those who are less fortunate in society. The play says “if sometimes we tried to put ourselves in the place of…”; the sheet shortens it
student_note: The Inspector tells the Birlings it would do us all good to show empathy to people less fortunate. He wants them to think about how others live.
techniques: Visual imagery / didactic appeal for radical empathy.
technique_notes: Goole explicitly models socialist empathy. Juxtaposing the minute domestic reality of “counting their pennies” in “dingy little back bedrooms” against Birling’s expansive wealth demands that the bourgeois elite look beyond abstract economic figures to acknowledge the claustrophobic lived reality of the working class.
context: Goole rebuking Birling’s lack of sympathy for his female factory staff.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges
sheet_note: Only on the mid-point sheet
student_note: The Inspector interrupts Mr Birling, who is boasting about his public status. He says that people with power and wealth have a duty to society as well as privileges.
technique_notes: Directly challenges the Edwardian social contract, asserting that civic honours, power, and wealth demand equal moral accountability to the public good.
context: Interrupting Birling’s attempts to invoke his civic status.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: We are members of one body
sheet_note: Only on the mid-point sheet
student_note: The Inspector says everyone in society is connected. We are all responsible for each other. This is a key message of the play.
technique_notes: Priestley appropriates Christian scripture to validate democratic socialism. Society is framed as an interdependent physical organism: harm inflicted on the most vulnerable part inevitably poisons and destroys the collective whole. | Metaphor – “members of one body”: Society is shown as a single body, so harming one part harms the whole. | Allusion – Echoes the Christian idea of the body of Christ: Priestley uses Biblical authority to support social responsibility.
context: The theological and political climax of Goole’s farewell sermon.

speaker: Mrs Birling
quote: You seem to have made a great impression on this child, Inspector.
sheet_note: Only on the mid-point sheet (first half of its quote 28)
student_note: Mrs Birling says this to Sheila, who is upset about Eva. She talks down to Sheila as if she is a child who doesn't understand.
techniques: Foils (Sheila and Mr Birling); Juxtaposition (the two generations’ values)
technique_notes: Foils – Sheila’s guilt is set against Mr Birling’s lack of guilt, so her moral growth stands out and the older generation looks stubborn. | Juxtaposition – Mrs Birling’s patronising “child” is opposed by the Inspector’s view that being “impressionable” is a moral virtue: the two generations’ values clash. | Adjective – “great”: shows how much Sheila has changed; she has made a real impact on the Inspector. | Mrs Birling uses the noun “child” to infantilise Sheila, attempting to dismiss her moral awakening as mere youthful fragility and keep her silenced within the domestic sphere. Inspector Goole subverts this condescension by reframing being “impressionable” as a vital moral virtue rather than a weakness. In the 1912 setting, Edwardian society demanded total obedience to patriarchal authority; for Priestley’s 1945 audience, Sheila’s generation was the one that lived through two catastrophic world wars caused by the hubris and complacency of men like Arthur Birling, and stood at the ballot box in 1945 to vote in a Labour government and establish the welfare state.
context: Early Act 2, when Mrs Birling enters the dining room and attempts to patronise Sheila’s emotional distress and growing sense of guilt.
lesson_techniques: Juxtaposition of Sheila (guilt) and Mr Birling (no guilt); “child” (Mrs Birling belittles and disempowers Sheila); Adjective “great” (shows how much Sheila has changed)

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: We often do on the young ones. They’re more impressionable.
sheet_note: Only on the mid-point sheet (second half of its quote 28)
student_note: The Inspector answers Mrs Birling. The young are more open to new ideas and feelings, and Priestley shows they are the hope for change.
techniques: Generational antithesis / patronising epithet vs moral validation.
technique_notes: Mrs Birling uses the noun “child” to infantilise Sheila, attempting to dismiss her moral awakening as mere youthful fragility and keep her silenced within the domestic sphere. Inspector Goole subverts this condescension by reframing being “impressionable” as a vital moral virtue rather than a weakness. In the 1912 setting, Edwardian society demanded total obedience to patriarchal authority; for Priestley’s 1945 audience, Sheila’s generation was the one that lived through two catastrophic world wars caused by the hubris and complacency of men like Arthur Birling, and stood at the ballot box in 1945 to vote in a Labour government and establish the welfare state.
context: Early Act 2, when Mrs Birling enters the dining room and attempts to patronise Sheila’s emotional distress and growing sense of guilt.
lesson_techniques: Juxtaposition of Sheila (guilt) and Mr Birling (no guilt); “child” (Mrs Birling belittles and disempowers Sheila); Adjective “great” (shows how much Sheila has changed)

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: Daisy Renton
sheet_note: Only on the mid-point sheet (the second name of the victim, part of its quote 17)
student_note: Eva Smith also used the name Daisy Renton. Two names make her stand for many working-class women, not just one person.
technique_notes: “Eva” recalls Eve (the biblical mother of all living humanity), while “Smith” is the most common British working-class surname, transforming her into an Everyman figure for the labouring masses. “Daisy” evokes a common, easily crushed field flower, while “Renton” hints at the financial desperation that forced her to rent out her body to survive.
context: The two names used by the victim across the narrative.
lesson_techniques: “Daisy” is a pretty flower (beauty, delicate and vulnerable; also a weed: common, insignificant, used by the upper classes); “Renton” (rent: a rip in fabric, how her life is torn apart)

speaker: Sheila
quote: If I could help her now – I would!
sheet_note: From Lesson 10 (young vs older generations): Sheila’s reaction, contrasted with Mr Birling’s “asking for the earth” line.
student_note: Sheila shows she feels guilty and wants to help. She is the opposite of Mr Birling, who asked for 'the earth'.

speaker: Sheila
quote: (with sharp sarcasm) You were the wonderful fairy prince
sheet_note: From Lessons 11 and 14: Sheila to Gerald about his affair with Daisy Renton.
student_note: Sheila speaks sharply to Gerald about his affair with Daisy Renton. She has become bold and no longer lets men control her.
lesson_techniques: Stage direction “sharp sarcasm”; Metaphor “fairy prince” (Gerald’s view of himself; also a fairy-tale or fantasy); Adjective “sharp”

speaker: Mrs Birling
quote: As if a girl of that sort would refuse money!
sheet_note: From Lesson 13: Mrs Birling on Eva’s refusal of the charity’s help. The play has “would ever refuse money”; the lesson omits “ever”.
student_note: Mrs Birling says a girl like Eva would never refuse money. She looks down on the poor and gets it wrong.
lesson_techniques: Derogatory language “that sort”; Imagery “girl”; Exclamative statement

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: You used her… as if she was an animal, a thing, not a person
sheet_note: From Lesson 14: the Inspector to Eric. The play has “Just used her for the end of a stupid drunken evening, as if she was an animal, a thing, not a person.”
student_note: The Inspector tells Eric he treated Eva like an animal, a thing, not a person.
lesson_techniques: Imagery “a thing”; Verb “used”; Animal imagery

speaker: Eric
quote: You killed her – and the child she’d have had too – my child
sheet_note: From Lesson 14: Eric to Mrs Birling.
student_note: Eric tells his mother she killed Eva and the grandchild Eva would have had. He is angry at her cruelty.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: One Eva Smith has gone but there are millions and millions and millions still left with us
sheet_note: From Lesson 15: the Inspector’s final speech. The play continues “of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us”; the lesson shortens it.
student_note: In his final speech, the Inspector says there are millions of people like Eva Smith. They are still suffering because of how others treat them.
lesson_techniques: Pronoun “us”; “Eva Smith” (represents all working-class people); Hyperbole

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: If men will not learn that lesson, they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish
sheet_note: From Lesson 15: the Inspector’s final speech. The play has “then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish”.
student_note: The Inspector warns that if people do not learn to look after each other, they will be taught in war. 'Fire and blood and anguish' suggests pain and suffering.
technique_notes: Imagery – “fire and blood and anguish”: Violent, painful images of war warn of the suffering that will follow if people ignore the lesson. | Metaphor – “taught it in fire and blood”: Learning is presented as punishment, with war as the teacher. | Dramatic irony – The 1945 audience has lived through two world wars, so they know the warning came true. | Audience – Written for people who had just experienced war, so the Inspector’s warning feels urgent and aimed at them.
lesson_techniques: Dramatic irony (the 1945 audience knew about the two world wars); Metaphor “lesson”; Hellish imagery

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: You’ll be able to divide the responsibility between you when I’ve gone
sheet_note: From Lesson 16 (accountability).
student_note: The Inspector tells the family they can divide up the blame. Each of them played a part in Eva's death.

speaker: Sheila
quote: I know I’m to blame – and I’m desperately sorry
sheet_note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz. In the play it continues “– but I can’t believe – I won’t believe – it’s simply my fault”.
student_note: Sheila says she knows she is partly to blame and is very sorry. She takes responsibility, unlike her parents.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: A girl died tonight… Died in misery and agony – hating life
sheet_note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz. The play has “A girl died tonight. A pretty, lively sort of girl… But she died in misery and agony – hating life”.
student_note: The Inspector reminds the family that a young woman died in misery and agony. He wants them to feel her suffering.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Impression of massiveness, solidity, and purposefulness
sheet_note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz: the stage direction describing the Inspector.
student_note: This stage direction describes the Inspector. He gives an impression of strength and solidity, and he seems serious and in control.

quote: I met a traveller from an antique land
student_note: The speaker does not see the statue himself. He only hears about it from a traveller.
technique_notes: Guide labels: adjective “antique”; the speaker does not see the statue, he only hears about it from the traveller.
lesson_techniques: Adjective “antique”; the speaker only hears about the statue from the traveller

quote: My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings
sheet_note: Shows the ruler’s arrogance and belief in his absolute power.
student_note: Ozymandias shows his arrogance and his belief that his power is absolute.
technique_notes: “King of Kings” emphasises superiority and dominance, reflecting extreme pride and hubris.
lesson_techniques: Religious imagery “king of kings”; symbol (Lesson: What does this symbol suggest?)

quote: Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
sheet_note: Shows how Ozymandias wanted others to fear and admire his power.
student_note: Ozymandias wanted others to fear and admire his power. It is ironic, because nothing of his power remains.
technique_notes: the commanding verb “Look” asserts authority, but it is ironic because nothing of his power remains. | Imperative – “Look”: The command shows the king’s arrogant authority, demanding attention and awe. | Irony – The “Mighty” are told to despair at his works, but only ruins remain: his power is gone.

quote: Nothing beside remains
sheet_note: Reveals that all of Ozymandias’ power and achievements have disappeared over time.
student_note: All of Ozymandias' power and achievements have disappeared over time.
technique_notes: the abruptness highlights emptiness, contrasting with his earlier arrogance.

quote: The lone and level sands stretch far away
sheet_note: Shows the vast, timeless power of nature compared to human power.
student_note: The vast, empty desert shows that nature lasts far longer than human power.
technique_notes: “lone and level” creates a sense of endless emptiness, emphasising how nature outlasts human ambition. | Imagery – “lone and level sands stretch far away”: Vast, empty desert imagery shows nothing is left of the king’s empire. | Alliteration – “lone and level”: The repeated “l” sound creates a flat, drawn-out effect that echoes the endless emptiness.
lesson_techniques: Symbol (Lesson: What does this symbol suggest?)

quote: Round the decay of that colossal wreck
student_note: The statue's proud words contrast with 'decay' and 'wreck'. The proud ruler has been destroyed.
technique_notes: Guide label: juxtaposition of what the statue says with “decay” and “wreck”.
lesson_techniques: Juxtaposition of what the statue says with “decay” and “wreck”

quote: Sneer of cold command
student_note: The statue's face shows a cold, commanding ruler. 'Cold' and the repeated 'c' sound make him seem harsh.
technique_notes: Lesson labels: the adjective “cold”; alliteration of “c”.
lesson_techniques: Adjective “cold” (also a cold body); alliteration of “c”

quote: Chartered streets
sheet_note: The anthology spells it “chartered” (the poem’s original has “charter’d”).
student_note: 'Chartered' means owned and controlled by someone. Even the streets and the river are controlled, which shows how trapped people are.
technique_notes: Guide labels (“chartered streets” and “chartered Thames”): adjective “chartered”; repetition; symbol of the river Thames.
lesson_techniques: Adjective “chartered”; repetition; symbol of the river Thames

quote: Mind-forg’d manacles
sheet_note: Shows how people are mentally trapped and controlled by society. The anthology spells it “mind-forged” (the original has “mind-forg’d”).
student_note: People are mentally trapped and controlled by society. 'Manacles' are chains, but these are in the mind.
technique_notes: “manacles” suggests imprisonment, while “mind-forg’d” implies people are trapped by their own thoughts or by society’s ideas, highlighting psychological oppression.
lesson_techniques: Metaphor “mind-forged manacles”; industrial imagery “forged”

quote: Runs in blood down palace walls
sheet_note: Suggests that the ruling classes are responsible for the suffering and deaths of ordinary people.
student_note: The ruling classes are responsible for the suffering and deaths of ordinary people. The blood is on the palace walls.
technique_notes: “blood” represents violence and sacrifice, while “palace walls” symbolise the monarchy, implying their power is built on the suffering of others. | Imagery – “blood” down “palace walls”: A vivid picture of violence staining the seat of power. | Symbol – “blood” represents violence and sacrifice; “palace walls” symbolise the monarchy, whose power is built on others’ suffering.
lesson_techniques: “Palace walls” = the monarchy as an oppressive institution; symbol of “walls”

quote: Blackning Church appalls
sheet_note: Critiques the Church for being corrupt and failing to help the poor.
student_note: Blake criticises the Church for being corrupt and failing to help the poor.
technique_notes: “blackning” suggests moral corruption, while the Church symbolises institutions that should protect people but instead contribute to their suffering.
lesson_techniques: “Blackning church” = the Church as an oppressive institution; adjective “blackning”

quote: Youthful Harlots
student_note: 'Harlots' means prostitutes. Blake uses them to show how poverty and society harm the young.
technique_notes: Guide label: symbol of “harlots”.
lesson_techniques: Symbol of “harlots”

quote: Small circles glittering idly
sheet_note: Shows the speaker’s arrogance at the start of the poem, as he disturbs the stillness of nature without thinking about the consequences.
student_note: At the start, the speaker is arrogant. He disturbs the stillness of nature without thinking about the consequences.
technique_notes: the ripples symbolise the way human actions disturb the natural world, while the repeated “s” sound creates a snake-like effect, suggesting temptation and foreshadowing his downfall. | Symbol – The “small circles” (ripples) symbolise the way human actions disturb the natural world. | Sibilance – The repeated “s” sounds create a snake-like effect, suggesting temptation and foreshadowing his downfall.
lesson_techniques: Symbolism of the ripples; sibilance; symbolism of stealing the boat; verb “glittering”

quote: The grim shape towered up between me and the stars
sheet_note: Shows the overwhelming and frightening power of nature as the mountain rises above the speaker and makes him feel small and powerless.
student_note: Nature feels overwhelming and frightening. The mountain rises above the speaker and makes him feel small and powerless.
technique_notes: the mountain is given a threatening presence through “towered,” while “grim shape” suggests fear and the unknown, emphasising the sublime power of nature. | Imagery – “grim shape towered”: A dark, looming image makes the mountain frightening and shows the power of nature. | Personification – The mountain “towered” as if it were chasing him, giving it a threatening presence.
lesson_techniques: Symbolism “stars”; verb “towered”; personification of the mountain; imagery “grim shape” (he cannot find the words); this is the volta

quote: Huge and mighty forms… were a trouble to my dreams
sheet_note: Shows that the experience has permanently changed the speaker, leaving him haunted and humbled by the power of nature.
student_note: The experience has changed the speaker for ever. He is haunted and humbled by the power of nature.
technique_notes: “huge” and “mighty” emphasise nature’s omnipotence, while “trouble to my dreams” shows that the encounter continues to disturb him psychologically.
lesson_techniques: Adjectives “huge” and “mighty”; symbolism “trouble”; imagery “forms”; symbolism “dreams”

quote: My Last Duchess
student_note: The Duke calls her 'my' Duchess, as if he owns her. She is known by her title, not her name.
technique_notes: Guide/lesson labels: possessive pronoun “my” (ownership); adjective “last”; the title “Duchess”; the Duchess is never given a name or voice.
lesson: Power and Conflict: My Last Duchess
lesson_techniques: Possessive pronoun “my”; adjective “last”; title “duchess”; she is never given a name or voice

quote: That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall
sheet_note: Shows how the Duke sees the Duchess as his possession rather than an independent person.
student_note: The Duke sees the Duchess as his possession, not as an independent person.
technique_notes: “my” suggests ownership and control, while “Duchess” reduces her to her status rather than her identity, showing how she is objectified and disempowered.

quote: I gave commands; then all smiles stopped together
sheet_note: Implied that the Duke had the Duchess killed because he was jealous and controlling.
student_note: This suggests the Duke had the Duchess killed because he was jealous and controlling. 'Commands' hides the brutality of what he did.
technique_notes: the vague phrase “gave commands” hides the brutality of his actions, while the pause emphasises the finality of her death. | Euphemism – “gave commands”: A vague phrase that hides the brutality of what the Duke actually ordered. | Caesura – The pause before “all smiles stopped” emphasises the finality of her death.

quote: Notice Neptune, though, taming a sea-horse
sheet_note: Shows the Duke’s obsession with control and power.
student_note: This shows the Duke's obsession with control and power. Neptune taming a sea-horse reflects how he wants to control others.
technique_notes: Neptune symbolises male power and domination, reflecting how the Duke sees himself as someone who should control others; the imperative “Notice” also reveals his arrogance and need to direct attention. | Symbol – Neptune taming a sea-horse symbolises male power and domination, the way the Duke sees himself. | Imperative – “Notice”: Shows his arrogance and his need to direct the listener’s attention.
lesson: Power and Conflict: My Last Duchess
lesson_techniques: Symbolism of the statue and of “Neptune”; he describes the statue like the painting

quote: Into the mouth of Hell
sheet_note: Shows the soldiers’ bravery as they charge into almost certain death.
student_note: The soldiers bravely charge into almost certain death. The battlefield is compared to hell.
technique_notes: compares the battlefield to “hell,” suggesting horror and sacrifice. The metaphor glorifies the soldiers’ courage while also showing the destructiveness and futility of war. | Metaphor – The battlefield is “the mouth of Hell”, suggesting horror and the destructiveness of war. | Symbol – “Hell” represents the suffering and futility of war, though the soldiers’ courage is also glorified.
lesson: Power and Conflict: The Charge of the Light Brigade
lesson_techniques: Hellish imagery; personification of the valley (“mouth”)
poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade

quote: Honour the Light Brigade, noble six hundred
sheet_note: Encourages readers to celebrate the soldiers’ bravery despite their pointless deaths.
student_note: Tennyson encourages readers to honour the soldiers' bravery, even though their deaths were pointless.
technique_notes: “Honour” and “noble” idealise the soldiers, reflecting patriotic pride and the way society glorifies sacrifice while ignoring the tragedy behind it.
lesson: Power and Conflict: The Charge of the Light Brigade
lesson_techniques: Double meaning of “light” (heaven, God), contrasted with “mouth of Hell”; semantic field of heroism (“honour”, “noble”); imperative
poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade

quote: Someone had blundered
sheet_note: The anthology has “Some one had blunder’d”.
student_note: Someone in command made a mistake. They are mentioned only in passing, while the soldiers are praised again and again.
technique_notes: Lesson labels: “someone” (those in command mentioned in passing) is juxtaposed with the repeated “noble six hundred”; the verb “blundered”.
lesson: Power and Conflict: The Charge of the Light Brigade
lesson_techniques: “Someone”: those in command mentioned in passing; juxtaposition with the “noble six hundred”; verb “blundered”
poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade

quote: Our brains ache
sheet_note: Shows shared exhaustion and suffering in harsh war conditions.
student_note: The soldiers share exhaustion and suffering in harsh war conditions.
technique_notes: “our” suggests unity and shared pain among soldiers, while “ache” captures the dull persistence of suffering from cold and fear. | Verb – “ache”: Captures the dull, persistent suffering from cold and fear. | Pronoun – “our”: Suggests unity and shared pain among the soldiers.

quote: The merciless iced east winds that knive us
sheet_note: Presents nature as the soldiers’ true enemy.
student_note: Nature, not the enemy, is the soldiers' real enemy. The wind is cruel, as if it is stabbing them with knives.
technique_notes: the wind is given human cruelty through “knive,” suggesting deliberate violence. Nature becomes a more relentless attacker than the soldiers’ human foes.
lesson_techniques: Personification of the weather (“merciless”, “knive”); sibilance; collective pronoun “us”

quote: All their eyes are ice
student_note: The soldiers' eyes are cold and lifeless. They have been dulled by the freezing cold and war.
technique_notes: Lesson labels (“Half-known faces. All their eyes are ice”): third-person pronoun “their”; symbol “eyes”; adjective “half-known”; metaphor “eyes are ice” (ice is brittle and fragile). | Metaphor – “eyes are ice”: Ice is brittle and fragile, suggesting the soldiers are frozen, numb and close to death. | Symbol – “eyes”: Represent the men’s inner lives, which are frozen and emptied by the war.
lesson_techniques: Third-person pronoun “their”; symbol “eyes” (windows to the soul); adjective “half-known”; metaphor “eyes are ice” (brittle, fragile)

quote: We are prepared: we build our houses squat
student_note: The islanders say they are ready for the storm. They have built their houses low and strong.

quote: Spits like a tame cat turned savage
student_note: The sea is compared to a tame cat turned savage. It looks calm but can suddenly become violent.
technique_notes: Guide labels: simile; juxtaposition of “tame” and “savage”. | Simile – “like a tame cat turned savage”: The sea, usually familiar and calm, suddenly turns wild and dangerous. | Juxtaposition – “tame” against “savage”: The contrast shows how quickly nature can turn from safe to threatening.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Storm on the Island
lesson_techniques: Simile; juxtaposition of “tame” and “savage”

quote: Blows full blast
student_note: The harsh 'b' sounds create the sound of the storm. 'Blast' suggests war.
techniques: Plosive consonants; Semantic field of war
technique_notes: Guide labels: plosive consonants create the sound of the storm; the semantic field of war (e.g. “blast”).
lesson: Power and Conflict: Storm on the Island
lesson_techniques: Plosive consonants; semantic field of war (“blast”)

quote: Bombarded by the empty air
student_note: The storm attacks like a war. 'Bombarded' is a violent verb, and the air seems empty yet dangerous.
technique_notes: Guide labels: violent verb “bombarded”; symbolism of the “empty air”.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Storm on the Island
lesson_techniques: Violent verb “bombarded”; symbolism of “empty air”

quote: King, honour, human dignity, etcetera
sheet_note: Mockingly lists patriotic values as meaningless in the panic of battle.
student_note: The poet mocks patriotic values. In the panic of battle, grand ideals become empty words.
technique_notes: placing grand ideals next to “etcetera” trivialises them, showing how war reduces noble motives to empty words.
lesson_techniques: Simile “dropped like luxuries”; juxtaposed with “etcetera” (sarcastic); list of “king”, “honour”

quote: Suddenly he awoke and was running
sheet_note: Shows the soldier’s panic and instinctive reaction.
student_note: This shows the soldier's panic. In war, instinct takes over from reason.
technique_notes: “Suddenly” and “running” create a sense of shock and chaos, reflecting how instinct takes over from reason during battle. | Verb – “running”: Shows instinct taking over in a sudden, frantic action. | Adverb – “Suddenly”: Creates a sense of shock and chaos.

quote: His terror’s touchy dynamite
sheet_note: Shows how fear turns the soldier into a weapon, ready to explode with violence.
student_note: Fear turns the soldier into a weapon, ready to explode with violence. 'Dynamite' makes him sound unstable and deadly.
technique_notes: the metaphor of “dynamite” turns the soldier into something unstable and deadly, while “touchy” suggests fragility and the uncontrollable power of fear.
lesson_techniques: Final line of the poem; alliteration of “t”; metaphor “dynamite”

quote: A yellow hare that rolled like a flame
student_note: The dying hare is described with violent, hellish imagery. 'Flame' makes the battlefield seem like hell.
technique_notes: Lesson labels: hellish imagery “flame”; violent imagery (a dying rabbit); symbolism of the “hare”.
lesson_techniques: Hellish imagery “flame”; violent imagery (a dying rabbit); symbolism of the “hare”

quote: His blood shadow
sheet_note: Shows how guilt and trauma follow the soldier after the killing.
student_note: Guilt and trauma follow the soldier after the killing. 'Shadow' suggests he can't escape it.
technique_notes: “blood” symbolises guilt and violence, while “shadow” suggests an inescapable reminder of his actions that haunts him psychologically. | Metaphor – “blood shadow”: The shadow is a metaphor for guilt that follows him everywhere. | Symbol – “blood” symbolises guilt and violence; “shadow” is an inescapable reminder that haunts him.
lesson_techniques: Metaphor “shadow”; metaphor (the stain of blood); violent imagery

quote: Probably armed, possibly not
sheet_note: Highlights uncertainty and guilt about whether the killing was justified.
student_note: The soldier is not sure if the killing was justified. This uncertainty leaves him full of guilt and doubt.
technique_notes: the contrast between “probably” and “possibly” captures the soldier’s doubt and the mental conflict that remains long after the event.
lesson_techniques: Repetition (repeated later when he returns home); syntax parallelism; adverb “possibly”

quote: Tosses his guts back into his body
sheet_note: Brutally describes the soldier cleaning up after the shooting.
student_note: This brutally describes the soldier cleaning up after the shooting. 'Tosses' sounds casual, showing how war makes soldiers numb.
technique_notes: “tosses” sounds casual and careless, showing how desensitised soldiers become; the graphic image reinforces the horror of war. | Imagery – “guts”: A graphic, shocking image that reinforces the horror of war. | Colloquial language – “tosses”: A casual, careless tone shows how desensitised soldiers have become.
lesson_techniques: Colloquial language (“my mate tosses his guts back into his body”)

quote: But I blink and he bursts again
student_note: When he closes his eyes, he remembers the soldier. The conflict is now in his mind.
techniques: Symbolism; Enjambment; Plosive consonants; Violent verb
technique_notes: Lesson labels: symbolism (when he closes his eyes he remembers the soldier); enjambment; plosive “b”; violent verb “bursts”.
lesson_techniques: Symbolism; enjambment; plosive consonants “b”; violent verb “bursts”

quote: End of story, except not really
student_note: This is the volta, the turning point of the poem. The conflict has moved from the battlefield to the soldier's mind.
technique_notes: Lesson: this is the volta; the conflict has moved from the battlefield to the soldier’s mind, and the poem focuses on the aftermath of war.
lesson_techniques: Volta

quote: On another occasion
student_note: The poem starts in the middle of the action. This suggests this is one of many stories that haunt the soldier.
technique_notes: Lesson: the poem starts in the middle of the action, suggesting this story is one of many that haunt the soldier.
lesson_techniques: In media res

quote: Spasms of paper red
sheet_note: Suggests both the delicate nature of the poppy and the pain of loss.
student_note: The poppy is delicate, but it also shows the pain of loss. 'Spasms' links remembrance to the bloodshed of war.
technique_notes: “spasms” implies both grief and violence, linking remembrance with physical pain and the bloodshed of war.
lesson_techniques: Symbolism of “red” and of “paper”; metaphor for a paper poppy; violent imagery “spasms”

quote: The gelled blackthorns of your hair
sheet_note: Shows both love and pain; motherhood mixed with sacrifice.
student_note: This shows both love and pain, with motherhood mixed with sacrifice. 'Blackthorns' recalls Christ's crown of thorns.
technique_notes: “blackthorns” recall Christ’s crown of thorns, symbolising suffering and sacrifice; “gelled” creates a tender, realistic image of her son.
lesson_techniques: Metaphor “blackthorns”; religious imagery; sensory imagery

quote: Running children in a nightmare heat
sheet_note: Refers to victims of war, showing the suffering caused by human conflict.
student_note: This refers to the victims of war. The children show innocence destroyed by violence.
technique_notes: “nightmare heat” evokes terror and pain; the children symbolise innocence destroyed by violence and humanity’s indifference to suffering. | Imagery – “nightmare heat”: Evokes terror and pain. | Symbol – The “running children” symbolise innocence destroyed by violence.
lesson_techniques: Metaphor “nightmare”; present continuous tense “running”; symbolism “children”; verb “running”

quote: In his darkroom he is finally alone
sheet_note: Shows his isolation and emotional distance from both his work and others.
student_note: The photographer is isolated and emotionally distant from his work and from others. The darkroom is also inside his mind.
technique_notes: the “darkroom” represents both his professional space and his internal world (inside his mind), where he must confront the moral weight of his photographs – his memories. | Juxtaposition – The quiet, private darkroom is set against the violence he has photographed, so he must face the moral weight of what he has seen. | Symbol – The “darkroom” represents both his professional space and his inner mind, where he confronts his memories.
lesson_techniques: Extended metaphor; “darkroom”; adjective “alone”

quote: Spools of suffering set out in ordered rows
sheet_note: Highlights the contrast between the chaos of war and the order of his work.
student_note: The photographs are compared to containers of human pain. Their neat arrangement contrasts with the chaos of war.
technique_notes: “spools of suffering” compares the photographs to containers of human pain; their careful arrangement shows his attempt to impose control over trauma.
lesson_techniques: Sibilance “spools of suffering”; “ordered rows”; Juxtaposition (from the revision sheet)

quote: Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.
student_note: A list of three places of conflict. The short sentences and hard 'b' and 'p' sounds sound like a list of horrors.
techniques: Caesura; Plosive consonants; List of three
technique_notes: Lesson labels: caesura; plosive consonants “b” and “p”; a list of three places of conflict.
lesson_techniques: Caesura; plosive consonants “b” and “p”; list of three (places of conflict)

quote: He earns his living and they do not care
student_note: The final line of the poem. It is matter-of-fact, and shows that people do not care about the suffering he photographs.
technique_notes: Lesson labels: declarative statement (matter-of-fact tone); the final line of the poem; collective pronoun “they”.
lesson_techniques: Declarative statement; final line of the poem; collective pronoun “they”

quote: Paper kites
Let the daylight break through capitals and monoliths
student_note: Light is set against hard stone. Daylight breaks through the hard buildings, which suggests freedom against control.
technique_notes: Lesson: the semantic field of light (“luminous”, “daylight”) against the semantic field of hard stone (“buildings”, “capitals”, “monoliths”).

quote: Pages smoothed and stroked and turned transparent with attention
There was once a country… I left it as a child
sheet_note: The anthology has “There once was a country…”; the revision guide has “There was once a country…”.
student_note: The poem begins by describing a country that is now in the past. The speaker left it as a child.
technique_notes: Guide labels: the past tense “There was once”; the caesura.
lesson_techniques: Past tense “There was once”; caesura

quote: It may be sick with tyrants, but I am branded by an impression of sunlight
sheet_note: Shows the speaker’s refusal to see her homeland negatively despite its political corruption.
student_note: The speaker refuses to see her homeland as bad, even though it is ruled by tyrants. Her happy memory of it is strong, like a brand.
technique_notes: contrasts “tyrants” with “sunlight,” suggesting memory is powerful and idealised; “branded” implies the memory is permanent. | Metaphor – “branded by an impression of sunlight”: The memory is burned into her, permanent. | Juxtaposition – “tyrants” against “sunlight”: Contrasts the country’s cruelty with her idealised, warm memory of it.
lesson_techniques: Imagery of “sunlight”; metaphor “branded”

quote: My shadow falls as evidence of sunlight
sheet_note: Shows how the speaker’s identity is shaped by her memories of her homeland.
student_note: The speaker's identity is shaped by her memories of her homeland. 'Sunlight' symbolises hope and positive memory.
technique_notes: “shadow” represents her presence and identity, while “sunlight” symbolises hope and positive memory; suggests that even in exile, her past continues to define her. | Metaphor – “my shadow falls as evidence of sunlight”: Her shadow is proof of the light, so even in exile her past defines her. | Symbol – “shadow” represents her presence and identity; “sunlight” symbolises hope and positive memory.

quote: It lies in front of me, docile as paper / I comb its hair and love its shining eyes
sheet_note: The anthology has “It lies down in front of me, docile as paper; / I comb its hair and love its shining eyes.”

quote: Bandage up me eye
student_note: 'Bandage up me eye' uses the Creole dialect 'me'. It is a metaphor for being blinded.
technique_notes: Guide labels: the metaphor of being blinded; the Creole dialect “me”.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History
lesson_techniques: Metaphor of being blinded; Creole dialect “me”

quote: Dem tell me
student_note: 'Dem' is Creole dialect for 'they'. The repetition shows how often people are told what to think.
technique_notes: Guide labels: the pronoun “dem”; repetition (“Dem tell me / Dem tell me”).
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History
lesson_techniques: Pronoun “dem”; repetition

quote: I carving out me identity
student_note: 'Carving' is a metaphor. The speaker is shaping her own identity with effort.
technique_notes: Guide label: the metaphor of “carving”.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History
lesson_techniques: Metaphor of “carving”

quote: Toussaint de thorn
technique_notes: Lesson slide: “What does this symbol suggest?”
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History
lesson_techniques: Symbol (lesson: what does this symbol suggest?)

quote: A healing star… a yellow sunrise
student_note: These images show hope and healing. They describe Mary Seacole.
technique_notes: Lesson slide: “What does this symbol suggest?” (about Mary Seacole).
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History
lesson_techniques: Symbol (lesson: what does this symbol suggest?)

quote: Head full of powerful incantations
sheet_note: Suggests the pilot is brainwashed by patriotic propaganda.
student_note: The pilot is brainwashed by patriotic propaganda. 'Incantations' compares it to spells.
technique_notes: “incantations” compares nationalistic ideas to spells, showing how the pilot’s thoughts are controlled by duty and expectation.
lesson_techniques: Hyperbole “full of”; metaphor “incantation” (magic spell); symbolism of the “shaven head”

quote: Fishes flashing silver
sheet_note: Represents the beauty of life that tempts the pilot to turn back.
student_note: The fish show the beauty of life that tempts the pilot to turn back. Silver shows purity and hope.
technique_notes: the image of “silver” symbolises purity and hope; the fish reflect the freedom and vitality of life, contrasting with his deathly mission.
lesson_techniques: Simile “like a huge flag”; metaphor “silver”; symbol of the “fishes” (the pilots); sibilance “fishes flashing silver”

quote: Which had been the better way to die
sheet_note: Shows how society’s rejection of the pilot is worse than dying in battle.
student_note: Society's rejection of the pilot is worse than dying in battle. It criticises the cruelty of shame and misplaced ideas of honour.
technique_notes: contrasts physical death with social death, criticising the cruelty of cultural shame and misplaced ideas of honour. | Juxtaposition – Physical death is set against social death, criticising the cruelty of cultural shame. | Rhetorical question – “Which had been the better way to die”: Makes the reader weigh the two kinds of death and question misplaced ideas of honour.
lesson_techniques: Final line of the poem; third person “he” (the daughter’s perspective); metaphorical “death”

speaker: Title
quote: The Modern Prometheus
sheet_note: The alternative title of the novel. Shelley compares Victor to the myth of Prometheus
student_note: This is the novel's subtitle. Shelley compares Victor to Prometheus, a figure from myth who stole fire from the gods and was punished.
context: Subtitle on the title page | Frankenstein lesson 1.
lesson_techniques: Allusion to Prometheus

speaker: Walton
quote: His limbs were nearly frozen
sheet_note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship
student_note: Walton describes Victor when he pulls him onto the ship. Victor is close to death.

speaker: Walton
quote: His body dreadfully emaciated
sheet_note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship
student_note: Walton describes Victor when he pulls him onto the ship. He looks starved and fragile.

speaker: Walton
quote: His eyes have generally an expression of wildness, even madness
sheet_note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship
student_note: Walton describes Victor's eyes, which look wild and even mad. Victor has been through a terrible ordeal.
context: Novel: "wildness, and even madness" | Frankenstein lessons 3 and 7: windows to the soul; Victor’s mind is broken.
lesson_techniques: Symbol “eyes”

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: My mother’s tender caresses and my father’s smile
sheet_note: Victor Frankenstein describes how his parents loved and cared for him
student_note: Victor describes how lovingly his parents cared for him.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was their plaything and their idol
sheet_note: Victor describes how his parents gave him a privileged and joyful childhood
student_note: Victor describes his happy, privileged childhood. His parents treated him like a toy and a precious object.
context: Frankenstein lesson 4: asked of the class.
lesson_techniques: Metaphor “plaything”, “idol”

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through
sheet_note: Victor describing his desire to create life and transgress the laws of nature and religion
student_note: Victor wants to create life. He sees life and death as boundaries he can break, against the laws of nature and religion.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: A new species would bless me as its creator and source
sheet_note: Victor hopes to create a new species of creatures that will recognise him as their God
student_note: Victor hopes to create a new species that will treat him like a god and be grateful to him as its creator.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I pursued nature to her hiding places
sheet_note: Victor describing how he seeks to transgress the laws of nature
student_note: Victor says he hunted nature down like prey. He is trying to break nature's laws to get what he wants.
context: Frankenstein lesson 5: nature is presented as prey to be hunted; Victor hunts down nature’s secrets.
lesson_techniques: Personification; Verb “pursued”

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I shunned my fellow creatures as if I had been guilty of a crime
sheet_note: Victor describing how isolated he became during the creation of the creature
student_note: Victor describes how isolated he became while he created the Creature. He avoided everyone.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Painful labour
sheet_note: Victor describing the hard work behind his creation of the creature
student_note: Victor describes the hard work of creating the Creature. 'Labour' also means childbirth, which links his work to giving birth.
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: childbirth imagery for the Creature’s birth.
lesson_techniques: Imagery (childbirth)

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The beauty of the dream vanished and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart
sheet_note: Victor describing how he is immediately disgusted by the creature and rejects it
student_note: Victor is disgusted as soon as the Creature comes to life. He rejects it immediately.
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: Victor’s horror and disgust.
lesson_techniques: Imagery (nightmare)

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Did I not as his maker owe him all the happiness that was in my power to bestow?
sheet_note: Victor agrees to make a female creature because he believes it’s his duty as his creator
student_note: Victor agrees to make a female creature because he feels it is his duty as the Creature's maker.
context: Novel: "all the portion of happiness that it was in my power to bestow"

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was a slave to my creature
sheet_note: Victor feels like he is controlled by the creature and must obey him
student_note: Victor feels controlled by the Creature and forced to obey him.
context: Novel: "the slave of my creature" (teacher: "a slave to my creature")

speaker: The Creature
quote: You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!
sheet_note: The Creature demands Victor to make him a female creature and tells him to obey
student_note: The Creature demands that Victor make him a female companion. He tells Victor he must obey because Victor owes him.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: No creature had ever been so miserable as I
sheet_note: Victor believes he is the most miserable living creature in existence
student_note: Victor believes he is the most miserable living creature that has ever existed.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: One by one, my friends were snatched away; I was left desolate
sheet_note: Victor describes how his loved ones have all been taken by the Creature, leaving him alone
student_note: Victor describes how the Creature has taken all his loved ones one by one, leaving him alone.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The death of William, the execution of Justine, the murder of Clerval, and lastly of my wife
sheet_note: Victor lists all the victims of the Creature
student_note: Victor lists the Creature's victims. Each death is a result of his own actions.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was the true murderer
sheet_note: Victor feels like he is truly responsible for the death of William and Justine
student_note: Victor feels he is truly responsible for the deaths of William and Justine, even though he did not do the killing himself.
context: Novel: "I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer" (also "But I, the true murderer" earlier in Chapter 8)

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I bore a hell within me which nothing could extinguish
sheet_note: Victor describing how the guilt he feels for the deaths of William and Justine is unbearable and will never go
student_note: Victor's guilt over the deaths of William and Justine is unbearable. He feels he carries hell inside him.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell
sheet_note: Victor describes how he aspired for power but it led to his downfall
student_note: Victor compares himself to Satan, the archangel who aspired to power. His ambition led to his downfall.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Demoniacal corpse
sheet_note: Victor describing the Creature, on the night he creates him
student_note: Victor describes the Creature on the night he creates him. The words make him sound like a dead body and a devil.
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: nightmarish imagery.
lesson_techniques: Imagery (nightmare)

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Begone! Vile insect!
sheet_note: Victor rejects the Creature when they meet on the mountain
student_note: Victor rejects the Creature when they meet on the mountain. He compares him to an insect, treating him as less than human.
technique_notes: Metaphor – “vile insect”: The Creature is compared to an insect, showing Victor sees him as disgusting and beneath him. | Imperative – “Begone!”: A harsh command that shows Victor’s rejection and fear.
context: Frankenstein lesson 15: Victor holds the power and dehumanises the Creature.
lesson_techniques: Imperative (command); Metaphor “insect”

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Monster
sheet_note: Victor describing the Creature. The Creature later calls himself this too
student_note: Victor calls the Creature a 'monster'. The Creature later uses the word about himself too.
context: Victor uses "monster" many times; first in Chapter 5

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Fiend
sheet_note: Victor describing the Creature. The Creature later calls himself this too
student_note: Victor calls the Creature a 'fiend', a devil. The Creature later uses the word about himself too.
context: "fiend" is used many times (e.g. Chapters 9, 16, 20)

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Demon
sheet_note: Victor describes the Creature
student_note: Victor calls the Creature a 'demon', an evil spirit.
context: 1818 text spells it "dæmon" (e.g. Chapter 7); used many times

speaker: William
quote: Ogre
sheet_note: William describing the Creature
student_note: William calls the Creature an 'ogre'. Even a child sees him as a monster and cannot be kind to him.
context: William says "ogre" in Chapter 16

speaker: Felix and Agatha
quote: Good spirit
sheet_note: Felix and Agatha believe that the Creature is a spirit helping their family
student_note: The cottagers believe the Creature is a kind spirit who helps their family. They do not know who he is.
context: Novel: "good spirit, wonderful" (the cottagers' words; Creature overhears)

speaker: The Creature
quote: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend
sheet_note: The Creature explains that he was once good, but his painful experiences have made him a monster
student_note: The Creature says he was once good, but pain and suffering made him a monster.

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: One hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me
sheet_note: Victor describing the Creature reaching out to him. He thinks it is trying to attack him
student_note: Victor sees the Creature reach out to him. He thinks the Creature is going to attack.

speaker: The Creature
quote: Barbarous villagers
sheet_note: The Creature describing the villagers who attacked him
student_note: The Creature describes the villagers who attacked him as savage and cruel.

speaker: The Creature
quote: The barbarity of man
sheet_note: The Creature describing the villagers who attacked him
student_note: The Creature says people can be cruel. He is attacked just for how he looks.

speaker: The Creature
quote: Low hovel
sheet_note: The Creature describing the hovel that becomes his home
student_note: The Creature describes the hovel that becomes his home. It is low, poor and dirty.

speaker: The Creature
quote: My kennel
sheet_note: The Creature describing the hovel that becomes his home
